h.strategy: Most obvious hypotheses follow a local story: an option matters more when its substitute is missing. These are usually rated likely and often fail. Instead, base hypotheses on robust statistical regularities. (1) Headroom: helpful edits help less in parents that are already strong, for example parents that already contain the strongest option elsewhere. (2) Harmful edits hurt more in strong parents and look harmless in weak parents, because of floor effects. (3) Saturation: adding a second copy of a strong option gives smaller gains than adding the first. (4) Removing an option costs less when the parent has several similar options. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy, so the effect is detectable. Cover several edited fields and both directions. In each 'why', state the obvious prediction and the reason the opposite should hold.

hyps.why: One might expect edge 4 to substitute for a removed edge 5, but strong parents have more accuracy to lose while weak parents sit near a floor.
One might expect a strong edge 5 to buffer a weak edge 4, but floor effects make harmful edits cost more in strong parents.
One might expect a strong neighbouring edge to compensate, but strong parents lose more from a harmful op because they sit far from the floor.
One might think a parameter-free skip is cheap to remove, but it is the cell's residual path and removing it degrades trainability most.
One might expect the removal to always hurt, but another identity-like path into the output makes the removed option redundant.
One might expect a weak parent to suffer more from a weak op, but node 2 is a dead end when edge 5 is none, so the harmful edit has no effect.
One might expect removing an edge to hurt more in an already sparse cell, but with edge 5 absent edge 1 cannot reach the output, so its removal is nearly free.
One might expect the conv to matter equally everywhere, but a direct conv to the output already makes the parent strong and leaves little headroom.
One might expect stacking convs into the output to help additively, but the already strong parent has less headroom.
One might expect convs to compound, but headroom means a parent that already has a 3x3 conv from the input gains less from another.
